title: The Price of Potatoes: a Guappo of the Corso Novara Market, and the Eighty Days of His Marriage
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Nolano and the Ration Books

stops.name: Palma Campania, the carter's son
stops.date_confidence: attested; English Wikipedia and italiamistero.it agree on the date and the town. Coordinates corrected from three disagreeing drafted values, two of which fell 3.5 km north-northwest in open country.
stops.campa: At the foot of Vesuvius, in a market town of the Nolano where every road carries produce down toward Naples, a carter's wife bears a son. They name him Pasquale Simonetti. The father hauls other men's crops for other men's money; the house is poor. The boy grows, and keeps growing, until his height is the first thing anyone says of him, nearly two meters in a country of short men. He is given twenty-nine years. He will spend nearly all of them within thirty kilometres of this house, taking a percentage of the produce that moves down these roads toward the city.
suggested_refs: Civil register of Palma Campania, February 1926, unconsulted

stops.name: Nola, the name he is given
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction; no source dates the nickname or names who first used it. The year is a placeholder for his adolescence in the Nola market circuit.
stops.campa: The town of Nola sits north of his birthplace, and its market is the hinge of the whole plain: potatoes, tomatoes, greens, moving by cart to the city. Simonetti works the circuit and the circuit names him. Pascalone 'e Nola, big Pasquale of Nola, though he was born at Palma Campania and no one records who first says it or when. The name outlives the man by seventy years. Neapolitan writers still use it for the type: the guappo who arbitrates a market he owns no part of.
suggested_refs: The wholesale produce market of Nola, hinge of the Nolano plain

stops.name: Naples, the falsified ration books
stops.date_confidence: attested only as 'the 1940s' by English Wikipedia and italiamistero.it; no source gives a year. 1943 is chosen for the fall of the regime and the arrival of the Allied administration, not because a source says so.
stops.campa: Mussolini's state has fallen and the Allied Military Government is counting what is left of a bombed city. Bread comes by annonaria, the ration book, and where there is a document there is a forger. Simonetti falsifies ration books and sells them into the Naples black market, which in these years is not a sector of the economy but the economy itself. Sources place this only in the 1940s and give no year. The racket is small and the man running it is seventeen years old. It is the first time his name attaches to the price of a scarce thing.
suggested_refs: Allied Military Government records on the Naples annona and ration-card fraud, 1943-1945, unconsulted

stops.name: Marseille, a port of the cigarette trade
stops.date_confidence: attested as a port of the postwar contraband trade, undated by the source. NOT attested as a place Simonetti went; an intermediate research pass wrongly read the ports as his own route.
stops.campa: Marseille is the first of four ports named in the record of the postwar cigarette trade, American and British tobacco moving into Naples by sea. The organisations that run it are Marseillais, Corsican and Sicilian, structured and foreign, and they do not come ashore themselves. They employ local guappi to distribute what lands. Simonetti belongs to that second class of men, the Neapolitan end of a Mediterranean line. No source puts him on a ship or in this city. The port stands for the trade that supports him, not for any voyage of his own.
suggested_refs: French customs and Sûreté files on the Marseillais tobacco trade, 1945-1955, unconsulted

stops.name: Gibraltar, the second port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: attested as a port of the trade, undated. Not attested for Simonetti personally; see the Marseille stop.
stops.campa: Gibraltar, a British rock at the mouth of the Mediterranean where goods change flag without changing hands, is the second port in the same sentence of the record. From here too the cases move east toward the Bay of Naples. The men who own the cargo are not the men who sell it in the Vasto; between the two stands a chain of distributors, and Simonetti is a link in it. The port matters because the trade is his living, not because he stood here; no source says he ever did.
suggested_refs: Colonial customs returns for Gibraltar tobacco re-export, late 1940s, unconsulted

stops.name: Nice, the third port of the trade
stops.date_confidence: attested as a port of the trade, undated. Coordinates corrected: the drafted pin sat 2.2 km southeast on Mont Boron rather than in the city.
stops.campa: Nice is the third port. The coast between here and Genoa is close enough to Italy that the customs line is a formality and far enough that the Italian police have no writ. Cigarettes leave; they arrive in Campania as merchandise with no origin. The distribution end, the end that carries the risk of arrest and the profit of a monopoly, sits in Naples with men like Simonetti. He is twenty years old. The last link in that chain, the one that meets both the buyer and the police, is where he stands.
suggested_refs: The port of Nice and the Ligurian contraband coast, 1945-1955

stops.name: Tangier, the fourth port
stops.date_confidence: attested as a port of the trade, undated; the source spells it 'Tangiers'. Coordinates corrected: the drafted pin sat 3.6 km northeast of the city.
stops.campa: Tangier is the fourth, an international free port where the law is written by committee and enforced by nobody. Tobacco leaves here for the whole northern shore. In the same years the Neapolitan quarter behind the central station absorbs what arrives, and the guappi of the Vasto take their percentage of every case. Simonetti will shortly leave tobacco for potatoes, a duller commodity with a better structure: potatoes have no legal substitute, they rot if they are not moved, and everybody in Campania eats them.
suggested_refs: Records of the Tangier International Zone administration on tobacco transit, unconsulted

stops.name: Torre Annunziata, where the cases come ashore
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and a weak one. No source names any landing point for Simonetti or for his associates; this is the regional pattern for the Campanian coast in these years and nothing more.
stops.campa: Between Torre Annunziata and Castellammare the coast runs flat and small boats can come in at night, which is why contraband on the Mediterranean route lands along this stretch in these years. Simonetti's home ground is half an hour inland. No source found names this beach, or any beach, for him: the landing point is a regional pattern and nothing else. It is marked here because the alternative is to draw a smuggling trade as though the goods arrived in Naples by post, and the gap is worth showing at its real size.
suggested_refs: Guardia di Finanza coastal seizure records for the Gulf of Naples, 1946-1952, unconsulted
sources: Gap: regional pattern only, not documented for Simonetti

stops.name: Port of Naples, Luciano comes ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested; inherited byte-identically from charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json.
stops.campa: By 1946 Naples is a bombed-out port city where the black market is the only economy that reliably pays, the same market Simonetti has been working since he forged ration books at seventeen. He is twenty now, moving from paper fraud into the cigarette trade that comes ashore through Marseille, Gibraltar, Nice and Tangier. The Vasto quarter behind the central station absorbs what lands, case by case, taking its percentage at every hand it passes through. He is still years from Corso Novara and the produce trade he will actually come to own.
suggested_refs: charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, Port of Naples stop

stops.name: Havana, Genovese crosses the water
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Havana meeting (Luciano file); the Naples connection is reconstruction. No document places Genovese and Simonetti together.
stops.campa: Vito Genovese crosses to Havana to propose to Luciano an arrangement over which of them is first. Genovese had spent 1943 and 1944 inside occupied Naples running black-market and currency operations for and against the Allied administration, and returned to America to face a murder charge he beat. The Naples he leaves behind is the Naples where Simonetti begins. The connection is adjacency and not evidence: no document places the two men in a room, and none is claimed here or implied by the pin.
suggested_refs: charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, Havana stop, 1946-12-22

stops.name: Via Tasso, the shop that is not a shop
stops.date_confidence: attested; inherited byte-identically from charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json.
stops.campa: Luciano opens a shop on Via Tasso selling appliances and sanitary goods. The police believe it is a front and that the money behind it is heroin. He will live at this address until he dies. Three kilometres east, in the same years, Simonetti is taking a hundred lire on every quintal of potatoes that crosses the Corso Novara market. Two economies of organised crime run in one city, one of them transatlantic and quiet, one of them local and loud, and neither of them appears anywhere in the other's file.
suggested_refs: charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, Via Tasso stop

stops.name: Naples Questura, the file that stays open
stops.date_confidence: attested for the Luciano interrogation; inherited from charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json. Nothing is attested about a Questura file on Simonetti, which is the point of the stop.
stops.campa: In these years the Naples Questura keeps files open on the guappi who set a price rather than take a wage, the same apparatus that processes every complaint the produce markets generate and settles almost none of them. Simonetti is by now established as one of three presidents of prices on the Nolano circuit, an arrangement the police tolerate without ever prosecuting it. No surviving record says what the Questura had gathered on him before July 1955, or when its attention on him began.
suggested_refs: Questura di Napoli files, 1948-1962, named as unconsulted in the Luciano dossier and unconsulted here

stops.name: Naples, soggiorno obbligato
stops.date_confidence: attested; the canonical atlas Naples pin, inherited byte-identically from charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, whose own note says it frames the planned Italian branch of this cluster.
stops.campa: Italian authorities impose soggiorno obbligato on Luciano, restricting him formally to Naples as a man considered mafioso and charged with nothing. It is November 1954. One month later Simonetti walks out of prison and finds that his partner has taken the business. Eight months after that he is dead on a street two kilometres from Luciano's shop. This coordinate already carries Virgil, Giordano Bruno, Jacques de Molay and Luciano among others; the guappo of the Nolano joins them at the same six decimal places.
suggested_refs: charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, soggiorno obbligato stop, 1954-11-01

stops.name: Corso Novara, the president of prices
stops.date_confidence: the year is a placeholder and no source supplies one; internapoli.it situates his market ascendancy only as postwar and before its early-1950s peak. Coordinates corrected: three drafted values for this street disagreed with each other and all three fell southeast of it.
stops.campa: East of the central station, in the Rione Vasto, the wholesale fruit and vegetable market of Corso Novara sets the price at which Campania eats. The men who set it are called presidents of prices. They are not elected. Simonetti becomes one of three, and takes a percentage of everything that moves through his territory. No source gives the year he arrives at the position; it is after the war and before the peak. The negotiation is conducted in the register of a favour that cannot reasonably be declined.
stops.quote: Guagliò, io devo spendere per voi dieci mila lire in fiori. Preferite i fiori per il funerale o per il matrimonio?
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Simonetti, quoted in Napolitan.it, 'La Camorra non perdona: la storia di Pascalone e Pupetta', 6 May 2015. Journalistic tradition: the outlet cites no trial or documentary source.
suggested_refs: The Corso Novara wholesale market in the Rione Vasto, Vicaria, Naples
sources: internapoli.it, 'Pascalone 'e Nola, così morì un guappo'

stops.name: Nola, one hundred lire the quintal
stops.date_confidence: attested as the height of his control, dated by sources only to the early 1950s.
stops.campa: At Nola the potatoes come in by the cartload, forty thousand quintals in a day at the height of it, and Simonetti takes a hundred lire on every quintal sold. Three to four million lire a day, by the accounts that circulate afterwards. He does not own a field, a lorry, or a stall. What he owns is the agreement that he is owed, and the certainty in every trader's mind about what happens to a man who tests it. The circuit runs from Nola through Pomigliano, Giugliano, Scafati, Pagani and Marano.
stops.quote: He was a tall man, nearly two meters, a gigantic man who always had a way of behaving, a 'guappaesica' way of doing things, a self-assured man
stops.quote_source: A contemporary, quoted in Felia Allum, 'The Neapolitan Camorra: Crime and politics in post-war Naples (1950-92)', PhD thesis, Brunel University, 2000, p. 370; seen via English Wikipedia, 'Pasquale Simonetti'. The thesis itself was not opened.
suggested_refs: Felia Allum, 'The Neapolitan Camorra' (Brunel PhD thesis, 2000), p. 370, unconsulted directly

stops.name: Pomigliano d'Arco, Totonno's ground
stops.date_confidence: attested as Esposito's base; the chronology of partnership turning to rivalry is undated in every source consulted and the two versions are not reconciled.
stops.campa: Pomigliano d'Arco is Antonio Esposito's ground, and Esposito is the man the market calls Totonno 'e Pomigliano: dried-fruit producer, president of prices, and a man with connections in politics that Simonetti does not have. English Wikipedia calls him a business partner who becomes a rival. internapoli.it calls him a competitor from the start. Nobody dates the turn, and neither account is preferred here over the other; both end in the same place.
suggested_refs: The dried-fruit trade of Pomigliano d'Arco and its political connections, 1950s

stops.name: Giugliano in Campania, Maisto's ground
stops.date_confidence: attested as Maisto's base; the year is a placeholder for the period before the 1952 fighting.
stops.campa: Giugliano in Campania belongs to Alfredo Maisto, the third of the price presidents, and he has no intention of yielding the Marano and Giugliano trade to a man from the Nolano. Three men now claim the right to set one price across one plain. Every trader on the plain can do that arithmetic, and so can the three men. The contest between them turns on one question: which of the three names can be spoken as a threat and be believed without anyone having to test it. Within a year it is being answered with pistols at Melito.
suggested_refs: terranostranews.it, 'Gomorra dalla A alla Z: Alfredo Maisto, Pasquale Simonetti e Antonio Spavone'

stops.name: Pagani, the far edge of the circuit
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the towns in the price circuit; no incident is dated here. Coordinates corrected: the drafted pin fell 1.2 km southwest, outside the town toward Sant'Egidio del Monte Albino.
stops.campa: Pagani lies at the far eastern edge of the circuit, in the province of Salerno, where the plain runs up against the Monti Lattari. Its produce trade is named in the list of towns that pass under the pricing system Simonetti comes to dominate. No incident is recorded here, no shooting, no meeting: the town marks reach rather than event. Campania in these years sends out something near a third of Italy's total output, and every quintal of it crosses a table where a percentage is understood.
suggested_refs: The Sarno valley produce trade and its wholesale intermediaries, early 1950s

stops.name: Marano di Napoli, the last of the towns
stops.date_confidence: attested as one of the towns in the price circuit; no incident is dated here.
stops.campa: Marano di Napoli closes the western end of the circuit, out past Giugliano toward the coast. Like Pagani it appears in the record as a name in a list, one of the towns whose fruit and vegetables move at a price no ministry sets. From Nola to Marano is thirty-five kilometres, an hour by cart and less by lorry. Inside that rectangle three men are collecting on the same commodity from the same growers, and by 1952 the arrangement between them has stopped being an arrangement at all.
suggested_refs: The Marano and Giugliano produce belt, contested ground between Simonetti and Maisto

stops.name: Melito di Napoli, the street gunfight
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1952 by internapoli.it and terranostranews.it; some derivative summaries move a similar incident to 1951 and the disagreement is left standing. The month is arbitrary. Coordinates corrected: the drafted pin fell 2.2 km west-northwest in Mugnano or Villaricca.
stops.campa: In the streets of Melito di Napoli, Simonetti's men and Alfredo Maisto's meet with pistols. Maisto sustains two armed confrontations in this year defending his ground against Simonetti and an associate named Raffaele Baiano. Some later summaries move the incident to 1951; the two Italian sources checked here both hold to 1952, and the disagreement is printed rather than settled. It is the first time the war over the price of potatoes is fought in daylight in front of witnesses who will be asked.
suggested_refs: Carabinieri and Questura reports on the Melito shootings of 1952, unconsulted

stops.name: Naples, eight years and three months
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1953 by English Wikipedia; no month, no day, and no court named beyond Naples. Canonical atlas Naples pin.
stops.campa: A court in Naples convicts him of attempted murder for the Melito shooting and sentences him to eight years and three months. No source names the courtroom or the judges; at this point the record thins to a number. He is twenty-seven years old. The market goes on setting its prices without him, and Antonio Esposito, who has been either his partner or his rival depending on which account is opened, takes over the joint business and keeps the receipts for the whole of the time he is away.
suggested_refs: The 1953 sentenza against Simonetti, court unidentified, unconsulted

stops.name: Poggioreale, the years inside
stops.date_confidence: INFERENCE, flagged. No source consulted places Simonetti at Poggioreale; the prison is documented for Maresca, not for him. Coordinates corrected: the drafted pin fell 1.6 km east, past the cemetery complex.
stops.campa: He serves his sentence in prison in Naples. Poggioreale is the city's prison and the obvious answer, but no source consulted actually places Simonetti inside it: the walls in this stop are an inference and the file says so plainly. What is attested is the arithmetic of the absence. Two years away from a market that ran on his physical presence is long enough for the arrangement to be rewritten by whoever stayed. He comes out owed money by a man who has decided in the meantime not to pay it.
suggested_refs: Registers of the Casa Circondariale di Poggioreale, 1953-1954, unconsulted
sources: Gap: prison not named for Simonetti in any source consulted
napolitan.it (for the release and the broken agreement)

stops.name: Naples, released at Christmas
stops.date_confidence: English Wikipedia gives 'Christmas 1954' and no exact date; 25 December is the atlas's reading of that phrase, not a sourced day.
stops.campa: At Christmas 1954, after roughly two of his eight years, Simonetti is released. Wikipedia gives the season and no date. He returns to a market where Esposito has taken the joint business and kept the profits, in breach of an agreement between men who never signed anything. There is no court for that debt. Across the city in these same weeks Charles Luciano is being confined to Naples by decree, an American with no charge against him and nowhere else he is permitted to go.
suggested_refs: charles_lucky_luciano.journey.json, soggiorno obbligato, November 1954

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the bride of the Lampetielli
stops.date_confidence: attested by it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' and English Wikipedia 'Pupetta Maresca'. An intermediate research pass carried the 1955 wedding date onto her birth as 27 April 1935, which is where the ubiquitous 'eighteen years old' comes from.
stops.campa: In Castellammare di Stabia, under Vesuvius on the far side of the bay, Assunta Maresca is born into the family the town calls the Lampetielli. She will be a beauty queen at eighteen and a widow at twenty, and she is the only person in this story whose own words survive in quantity. Nearly every retelling makes her eighteen at her wedding by moving her birth onto the wedding's date. She was born in January 1935 and was twenty; the arithmetic, corrected here, is worth keeping visible.
suggested_refs: Civil register of Castellammare di Stabia, January 1935, unconsulted

stops.name: Palma Campania, five hundred guests
stops.date_confidence: attested by three sources on both date and town. Two intermediate entries wrongly moved the ceremony to the Pompei sanctuary and a third to Naples.
stops.campa: Simonetti marries Assunta Maresca in his own town. Five hundred guests come, among them Alfredo Maisto and Antonio Esposito, the two men who have spent three years trying to take his trade; one account has Esposito standing as witness and ring-bearer, though it is thinly sourced. The whole of Palma Campania takes part. Envelopes of money change hands in the customary way. She is already pregnant. From this day to the day he is shot on Corso Novara is eighty days, and the count is exact.
suggested_refs: Parish marriage register, Palma Campania, 27 April 1955, unconsulted

stops.name: Pompei, the pistol left at the sanctuary
stops.date_confidence: attested by napolitan.it as a post-ceremony visit, single source. This is NOT the wedding venue; the marriage was celebrated at Palma Campania.
stops.campa: After the ceremony the couple go down to the Marian sanctuary at Pompei, the great pilgrimage church raised beside the excavated Roman streets. There, by the account that survives, Simonetti hands his wife his pistol and leaves it as a votive offering, a promise to change his life. Nothing in the record says what she did with it afterwards. Eighty days later she is looking for another one. Several retellings move the marriage itself to this altar; the marriage was at Palma Campania and this was the visit after.
suggested_refs: Santuario della Beata Vergine del Rosario, Pompei, ex-voto records, unconsulted

stops.name: Corso Novara, the greeting not returned
stops.date_confidence: 16 July is attested by both English Wikipedia articles, terranostranews.it and italiamistero.it, and confirmed arithmetically by the eighty days from the wedding; it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' gives 15 July and is left standing as a dissent. The failed-greeting trigger comes from internapoli.it alone.
stops.campa: On Corso Novara, in the morning, near the market he presides over, Simonetti meets Carlo Gaetano Orlando, called Tanino 'e Bastimento. By the one account that supplies a trigger, Orlando does not return the customary greeting. The failure is not an oversight and both men know what it announces. Orlando shoots him in the abdomen in broad daylight and walks away. He is acting on Antonio Esposito's orders, and the thing this is about is the fruit and vegetable market a hundred metres from where he falls.
suggested_refs: Questura di Napoli file on the Corso Novara shooting of 16 July 1955, unconsulted

stops.name: Ospedale degli Incurabili, the peritonitis
stops.date_confidence: CONTRADICTION, unresolved. internapoli.it alone separates the shooting (16 July) from death by peritonitis (17 July); English Wikipedia and italiamistero.it collapse both into 16 July; it.wikipedia 'Assunta Maresca' gives 15 July. The atlas takes internapoli.it and prints the disagreement.
stops.campa: He is carried to the Ospedale degli Incurabili, a hospital in the old city that has been taking in the wounded of Naples since the sixteenth century. They operate. Peritonitis follows. His wife reaches the bed and he names Esposito to her as the man who ordered it, and then he dies. The sources split three ways on the date: the sixteenth, the fifteenth, or the shooting on the sixteenth and the death on the seventeenth. The last of the three is used here, and the split is printed rather than averaged.
stops.quote: Corsi subito all'ospedale Incurabili dove l'avevano portato. L'avevano operato, ma era subentrata la peritonite. Mi rincuorava e mi fece il nome di Esposito come mandante della sparatoria. Pascalone era il mio principe azzurro e io volevo che si facesse giustizia, ma la giustizia voleva prove, prove, prove
stops.quote_source: Assunta 'Pupetta' Maresca, quoted by Gigi Di Fiore, Il Mattino, 16 July 2005, republished at Internapoli.it. Her recollection decades later of his dying words, not a transcript of Simonetti.
suggested_refs: Ospedale degli Incurabili admission and mortuary records, July 1955, unconsulted
sources: internapoli.it, reproducing Gigi Di Fiore, Il Mattino, 16 July 2005

stops.name: Naples, the funeral no one wrote down
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION. No source consulted gives the funeral's date, church, route, or size. The date is a placeholder three days after the death and should not be quoted as fact.
stops.campa: A guappo of his standing is buried in front of a crowd. Nothing else can be said. No source found in this research gives the church, the route, the date, or the number of people who walked behind him, and the honest form of this stop is the shape of the hole in it. What the record preserves instead is what the newspapers went looking for: not the funeral of the man who set the price of potatoes, but the widow, twenty years old and six months pregnant, photographed in black.
suggested_refs: Neapolitan press of 18-21 July 1955, unconsulted; would settle the funeral question
sources: Gap: no funeral detail found in any source consulted

stops.name: Palma Campania, a grave with no record
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION, and the weakest stop in the file. No cemetery record, headstone, or source names his burial place; custom alone puts him at Palma Campania or Nola.
stops.campa: Custom would put him in the ground at Palma Campania or at Nola, among his own people. No cemetery record has been found, no headstone photographed, no source consulted names the plot or the parish. The town is marked here as a guess, not a record. Seventy years of retelling have produced a film, a television miniseries, two novels and a shelf of true-crime articles about the eighty days of his marriage, and not one line among them that says where the body is.
suggested_refs: Cemetery registers of Palma Campania and Nola, unconsulted
sources: Gap: no burial record found in any source consulted

stops.name: Corso Novara, the Bar Grandone
stops.date_confidence: 4 October is given by it.wikipedia, napolitan.it, English Wikipedia 'Pasquale Simonetti', storienapoli.it and Il Mattino, and fits the eighty-day interval from 16 July and the arrest ten days later. 4 August recurs independently in internapoli.it and English Wikipedia 'Pupetta Maresca' and is not dismissed; a stray 16 September also circulates. Bar Grandone stood on Corso Novara, not in Piazza Garibaldi.
stops.campa: Eighty days after the killing, dressed in mourning and six months pregnant, Assunta Maresca takes a taxi with her brother Ciro to the Bar Grandone on Corso Novara and shoots Antonio Esposito dead. She holds the revolver in both hands. Accounts give twenty-nine shots from a Smith and Wesson .38; investigators concluded the shots came from at least four pistols, and both versions are still in print. Her husband was shot on this street in July. The answer to it happens on the same paving.
stops.quote: I was afraid I would miss
stops.quote_source: Assunta 'Pupetta' Maresca, her later explanation for firing two-handed, quoted in English Wikipedia 'Pupetta Maresca' from The Times (20 April 1959) and Fiandaca (ed.), 'Women and the Mafia' (2007), p. 12. Neither was opened directly.
suggested_refs: Fiandaca (ed.), 'Women and the Mafia' (Springer, 2007), p. 12, unconsulted

stops.name: Poggioreale, the arrest
stops.date_confidence: attested; sources give either 13 or 14 October 1955, and it.wikipedia and English Wikipedia agree on the 14th. Coordinates corrected as at the earlier Poggioreale stop.
stops.campa: Maresca is arrested ten days after the killing and taken to Poggioreale. Sources give the thirteenth or the fourteenth of October. She does not deny it and never will deny it. The Italian press has already begun turning a widow into an archetype, the lady camorrista, and the country will still be arguing about her when she dies at eighty-six. The man she did it for has been dead three months, buried nobody records where, and from here on the press mentions him mainly as her reason.
suggested_refs: Arrest and custody records, Poggioreale, October 1955, unconsulted

stops.name: Poggioreale, the son born inside
stops.date_confidence: RECONSTRUCTION. No source gives a birth date, and napolitan.it names no facility beyond 'prison'. The year is counted forward from an October arrest at six months; naming Poggioreale is a second inference on top of the first.
stops.campa: Inside the prison infirmary Maresca gives birth to Simonetti's son, born after his father's death and given his father's name. No source supplies a date. No source names the facility beyond the word prison; Poggioreale is where she was taken at her arrest and the inference stops at that. The birth year given here, 1956, comes from counting forward from an October arrest at six months along: arithmetic rather than anybody's record, though the name given to the boy, Pasquale, was never in question.
suggested_refs: Prison infirmary birth records, Naples, 1956, unconsulted

stops.name: Castel Capuano, the Corte d'Assise
stops.date_confidence: the trial is attested to April 1959 by both English Wikipedia articles, which give no day; 7 April is the date of the New York Times report and is used here as the anchor. The NYT archive page was not opened.
stops.campa: The Court of Assizes of Naples sits at Castel Capuano, a Norman castle turned courthouse, and the trial of Assunta Maresca runs thirty-three hearings through the spring. Foreign correspondents come. The New York Times debates whether Italy has a law of honour and what a jury is going to do with a widow. She tells the court she would repeat it, and the courtroom cheers her. Her husband, four years dead by now, is spoken of throughout as the reason and is not otherwise discussed.

stops.name: Castel Capuano, the verdict at 23:15
stops.date_confidence: attested by napolitan.it and it.wikipedia, including the hour and the twelve hours of deliberation. The date of the later appeal reduction is not given by anything consulted.
stops.campa: At a quarter past eleven at night, after twelve hours of deliberation, the court delivers: thirty years for Gaetano Orlando, who shot Simonetti; eighteen years and six months for Assunta Maresca; twelve years and four months for her brother Ciro. On appeal her sentence falls to thirteen years and four months with lifetime disqualification from public office, on a date that no source consulted supplies. Nobody is convicted of ordering Simonetti's death. The man who ordered it has been dead since October 1955.

One source gives the day, the seventeenth of April 1965, and nothing else corroborates it; the others give only the year. She is thirty years old. Her husband has been dead a decade and has become a character: Vito Polara in Rosi's film, a name in songs, the first half of a story whose second half is her. She will live another fifty-six years and every one of them will be reported as an appendix to eighty days in 1955.

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the widow dies
stops.date_confidence: attested by ANSA and Fanpage. An intermediate draft folded this together with the funeral ban of 1 January 2022; they are two separate dated events.
stops.campa: Assunta Maresca dies at Castellammare di Stabia, in the town she was born in, at eighty-six. The obituaries in the Italian press run long and reach for the same phrase, the first lady camorrista, an archetype that did not exist before an afternoon on Corso Novara in 1955. The ANSA headline says she died forgotten. She had outlived her husband by sixty-six years, which is more than twice as long as he was alive, and every notice of her death names him in its first paragraph.

stops.name: Castellammare di Stabia, the funeral forbidden
stops.date_confidence: attested; ANSA, Fanpage and Il Fatto Quotidiano all report the ban on 1 January 2022, the morning the rite had been scheduled.
stops.campa: The funeral is set for the morning of the first of January at Sant'Antonio di Padova. The Prefect and the Questore of Naples forbid it, fearing the rite becomes a spectacle, and authorise only a blessing of the remains at the cemetery. About ten women go to the church anyway and pray. Her lawyers object publicly that calling her a camorrista is defamatory. Simonetti's own funeral, sixty-six years earlier, went unrecorded. Hers is on the record because the state refused to allow it.
